newsitem.title: USA: Los Angeles County tax shift ruling raises concern.
newsitem.headline: Los Angeles County tax shift ruling raises concern.

text.p: A judge in California has ruled that legislation that helped cash-strapped Los Angeles County balance its budget violated the state's Constitution, prompting some concern Wednesday among credit analysts.
The ruling also attracted the attention of Orange County's attorneys and advisers because similar legislation helped Orange County emerge from bankruptcy earlier this year.
Wednesday, the attorney who filed the Los Angeles suit said he may now file a similar action against Orange County.
The 1995 fiscal relief legislation authorized the transfer of $50 million of Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority sales tax funds to the county.

Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Richard Hubbell ruled, however, that the legislation that allowed Los Angeles County to take the money violated a provision of the state Constitution that prohibits special statutes for the benefit of a county or city. The ruling was made public Tuesday.
Rating agency officials expressed some concerns Wednesday and said they would review the decision closely.
"We'll certainly look into this," said Moody's Investors Service Inc vice president Ken Kurtz. "It's a significant amount of money, but it's not a disastrous amount."
"We'll be interested in the ruling when we see it," said Standard & Poor's Corp director David Hitchcock. "We look at everything that seems significant."

The decision was a setback for Los Angeles County, which sought the transit funds during its budget crisis last year, county officials said. County attorneys said, however, that the trial court's action would be stayed pending an appeal.
"We'll see them on appeal," said Zev Yaroslavsky, chairman of Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors. "Until the appeals are resolved, we have no intention of addressing the pay back issue."
Yaroslavsky added, "The money has been spent already. If it (the ruling) holds, it would have draconian implications for Los Angeles and Orange County."

Hubbell's decision came out of a trial that took place in late November in response to a taxpayer lawsuit filed by Los Angeles attorney Richard Fine. The lawsuit sought the return of the taxpayer money to the transportation authority.

"We've won a number of similar cases, and in each case the court's decision has sent a message to our politicians: You can't continue to spend taxpayers' money to bail out a government when those responsible for its fiscal health fail in their responsibilities," Fine said.
Fine added he may now challenge the Orange County legislation on similar grounds.

"We're reviewing the Orange County legislation right now," Fine said. "It's similar (to the Los Angeles County legislation) in the sense that it states that it is special legislation to relieve the fiscal crisis in Orange County. We'll make our decision in the next couple of days."
He said Orange County should never have sought this type of legislation, which diverts transit and other funds to help repay county bondholders.

"They never should have put this type of legislation into their bankruptcy plan," Fine said. "If it forces them into bankruptcy (again), it is a problem they will have to face because they knew at the time that they passed this legislation that it could be unconstitutional."
